tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.

- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

"""Estimate elastic modulus for each material from tensile test data.

Fits a straight line (stress = E * strain + b) to each specimen and to the
pooled data for each material, then plots the data with the pooled fits.
"""

import json
import os

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

DATA_PATH = "measurements.csv"
SPECIMEN_RESULTS_PATH = "results/moduli-by-specimen.csv"
MATERIAL_RESULTS_PATH = "results/moduli.csv"
SUMMARY_PATH = "results/summary.json"
FIG_PATH = "figures/stress-strain.png"

# Materials in a fixed order so colors always follow the material
MATERIALS = ["steel", "titanium", "aluminum"]
COLORS = {"steel": "#2a78d6", "titanium": "#eb6834", "aluminum": "#1baf7a"}
MARKERS = ["o", "s", "^"]


def linear_fit(strain, stress):
    """Least-squares fit of stress = slope * strain + intercept.

    Returns slope, intercept, standard error of the slope, and R^2.
    """
    x = np.asarray(strain, dtype=float)
    y = np.asarray(stress, dtype=float)
    n = len(x)
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
    resid = y - (slope * x + intercept)
    ss_res = np.sum(resid**2)
    ss_tot = np.sum((y - y.mean()) ** 2)
    slope_se = np.sqrt(ss_res / (n - 2) / np.sum((x - x.mean()) ** 2))
    return slope, intercept, slope_se, 1 - ss_res / ss_tot


df = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH)
os.makedirs("results", exist_ok=True)
os.makedirs("figures", exist_ok=True)

# Per-specimen fits (stress in MPa, so slope / 1000 gives GPa)
rows = []
for (material, specimen), g in df.groupby(["material", "specimen"]):
    slope, intercept, slope_se, r2 = linear_fit(g.strain, g.stress_mpa)
    rows.append(
        {
            "material": material,
            "specimen": specimen,
            "n_points": len(g),
            "modulus_gpa": slope / 1e3,
            "modulus_se_gpa": slope_se / 1e3,
            "intercept_mpa": intercept,
            "r_squared": r2,
        }
    )
by_specimen = pd.DataFrame(rows)
by_specimen.round(4).to_csv(SPECIMEN_RESULTS_PATH, index=False)

# Per-material: mean and spread of specimen moduli, plus a pooled fit
rows = []
pooled_fits = {}
for material in MATERIALS:
    g = df[df.material == material]
    s = by_specimen[by_specimen.material == material]
    slope, intercept, slope_se, r2 = linear_fit(g.strain, g.stress_mpa)
    pooled_fits[material] = (slope, intercept)
    rows.append(
        {
            "material": material,
            "n_specimens": len(s),
            "modulus_mean_gpa": s.modulus_gpa.mean(),
            "modulus_std_gpa": s.modulus_gpa.std(ddof=1),
            "modulus_min_gpa": s.modulus_gpa.min(),
            "modulus_max_gpa": s.modulus_gpa.max(),
            "modulus_pooled_gpa": slope / 1e3,
            "modulus_pooled_se_gpa": slope_se / 1e3,
            "intercept_pooled_mpa": intercept,
            "r_squared_pooled": r2,
        }
    )
by_material = pd.DataFrame(rows)
by_material.round(4).to_csv(MATERIAL_RESULTS_PATH, index=False)

with open(SUMMARY_PATH, "w") as f:
    json.dump(
        {
            "materials": by_material.to_dict(orient="records"),
            "specimens": by_specimen.to_dict(orient="records"),
            "strain_range": [float(df.strain.min()), float(df.strain.max())],
        },
        f,
        indent=2,
    )

# Figure: data by specimen with pooled linear fit per material
plt.rcParams.update({"font.size": 10, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.8), dpi=200)
x_fit = np.linspace(0, df.strain.max() * 1.02, 50)
for material in MATERIALS:
    color = COLORS[material]
    g = df[df.material == material]
    for marker, (specimen, gs) in zip(MARKERS, g.groupby("specimen")):
        ax.scatter(
            gs.strain * 100,
            gs.stress_mpa,
            s=22,
            marker=marker,
            facecolor=color,
            edgecolor="white",
            linewidth=0.6,
            alpha=0.9,
            zorder=3,
            label=f"{specimen}",
        )
    slope, intercept = pooled_fits[material]
    ax.plot(x_fit * 100, slope * x_fit + intercept, color=color, lw=1.5, zorder=2)
    row = by_material[by_material.material == material].iloc[0]
    ax.annotate(
        f"{material.capitalize()}\nE = {row.modulus_mean_gpa:.0f} ± "
        f"{row.modulus_std_gpa:.0f} GPa",
        xy=(x_fit[-1] * 100, slope * x_fit[-1] + intercept),
        xytext=(6, 0),
        textcoords="offset points",
        va="center",
        fontsize=9,
        color="#0b0b0b",
    )
ax.set_xlabel("Strain (%)")
ax.set_ylabel("Stress (MPa)")
ax.set_xlim(0, None)
ax.set_ylim(0, None)
ax.grid(True, color="#e4e3df", lw=0.6, zorder=0)
ax.tick_params(colors="#52514e")
ax.set_title(
    "Tensile stress vs. strain with linear fits", loc="left", fontsize=11
)
ax.legend(
    title="Specimen", ncol=3, fontsize=8, title_fontsize=8, frameon=False,
    loc="upper left",
)
fig.subplots_adjust(right=0.78)
fig.savefig(FIG_PATH, bbox_inches="tight")
print(by_material.round(3).to_string(index=False))
print(by_specimen.round(3).to_string(index=False))
EOF

import json

SUMMARY_PATH = "results/summary.json"
REPORT_PATH = "report.md"
FIG_PATH = "figures/stress-strain.png"

# Typical handbook values for context (GPa)
REFERENCE_MODULI = {
    "steel": "190–210",
    "titanium": "105–120 (e.g., Ti-6Al-4V ≈ 114)",
    "aluminum": "68–72",
}

with open(SUMMARY_PATH) as f:
    summary = json.load(f)

specimens = summary["specimens"]
strain_min, strain_max = summary["strain_range"]
n_points = specimens[0]["n_points"]
r2_min = min(s["r_squared"] for s in specimens)
max_abs_intercept = max(abs(s["intercept_mpa"]) for s in specimens)
max_cv = max(m["modulus_std_gpa"] / m["modulus_mean_gpa"] for m in materials)

stiffest, _, softest = materials
ratio = stiffest["modulus_mean_gpa"] / softest["modulus_mean_gpa"]

material_rows = "\n".join(
    f"| {m['material'].capitalize()} | {m['n_specimens']} "
    f"| **{m['modulus_mean_gpa']:.1f} ± {m['modulus_std_gpa']:.1f}** "
    f"| {m['modulus_min_gpa']:.1f}–{m['modulus_max_gpa']:.1f} "
    f"| {m['r_squared_pooled']:.4f} "
    f"| {REFERENCE_MODULI[m['material']]} |"
    for m in materials
)
specimen_rows = "\n".join(
    f"| {s['specimen']} | {s['material']} | {s['modulus_gpa']:.1f} "
    f"| {s['modulus_se_gpa']:.1f} | {s['intercept_mpa']:.2f} "
    f"| {s['r_squared']:.4f} |"
    for s in sorted(specimens, key=lambda s: s["specimen"])
)

report = f"""# Elastic modulus from tensile test data

## Method

The data in `measurements.csv` are stress (MPa) vs. strain for three
specimens each of steel, titanium, and aluminum, with {n_points} points per
specimen over strains of {strain_min * 100:.2f}–{strain_max * 100:.2f}%.
For each specimen I fit a straight line, stress = *E* · strain + *b*, by
ordinary least squares. The slope *E* is the elastic (Young's) modulus.
Each material's modulus is reported as the mean ± sample standard deviation
of its three specimen moduli. A pooled fit of all of a material's points
gives the same slope, because all specimens were measured at the same
strains.

## Results

| Material | Specimens | *E* (GPa), mean ± SD | Specimen range (GPa) | Pooled *R*² | Typical handbook value (GPa) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{material_rows}

![Stress vs. strain with linear fits]({FIG_PATH})

*Figure: Measured stress vs. strain for each specimen (markers) with the
pooled linear fit for each material (lines).*

## Discussion

- **Ranking:** {stiffest['material']} is the stiffest material, about
  {ratio:.1f}× stiffer than {softest['material']}. All three moduli fall
  within the typical handbook ranges for these materials.
- **Linearity:** Each specimen is well described by a straight line
  (*R*² ≥ {r2_min:.3f}). The intercepts are all small
  (|*b*| ≤ {max_abs_intercept:.1f} MPa), so the fits pass close to the
  origin, as expected for linear elastic loading. The residuals look like
  random scatter with no curvature, so the data show no sign of yielding
  over this strain range.
- **Repeatability:** The specimen-to-specimen spread is small: the
  coefficient of variation is at most {max_cv * 100:.1f}% for any material.
  With only three specimens per material, the standard error of each mean
  is roughly SD/√3 ≈ 1 GPa.

## Per-specimen fits

| Specimen | Material | *E* (GPa) | Std. error of slope (GPa) | Intercept (MPa) | *R*² |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{specimen_rows}

Full results: `results/moduli.csv` (by material) and
`results/moduli-by-specimen.csv` (by specimen).
"""

with open(REPORT_PATH, "w") as f:
    f.write(report)

The data in `measurements.csv` are stress (MPa) vs. strain for three
specimens each of steel, titanium, and aluminum, with 10 points per
specimen over strains of 0.02–0.20%.
For each specimen I fit a straight line, stress = *E* · strain + *b*, by
ordinary least squares. The slope *E* is the elastic (Young's) modulus.
Each material's modulus is reported as the mean ± sample standard deviation
of its three specimen moduli. A pooled fit of all of a material's points
gives the same slope, because all specimens were measured at the same
strains.

## Results

| Material | Specimens | *E* (GPa), mean ± SD | Specimen range (GPa) | Pooled *R*² | Typical handbook value (GPa) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Steel | 3 | **199.1 ± 2.0** | 197.3–201.2 | 0.9984 | 190–210 |
| Titanium | 3 | **116.6 ± 1.7** | 114.6–117.8 | 0.9979 | 105–120 (e.g., Ti-6Al-4V ≈ 114) |
| Aluminum | 3 | **69.4 ± 1.8** | 67.4–70.6 | 0.9983 | 68–72 |

![Stress vs. strain with linear fits](figures/stress-strain.png)

*Figure: Measured stress vs. strain for each specimen (markers) with the
pooled linear fit for each material (lines).*

## Discussion

- **Ranking:** steel is the stiffest material, about
  2.9× stiffer than aluminum. All three moduli fall
  within the typical handbook ranges for these materials.
- **Linearity:** Each specimen is well described by a straight line
  (*R*² ≥ 0.998). The intercepts are all small
  (|*b*| ≤ 2.2 MPa), so the fits pass close to the
  origin, as expected for linear elastic loading. The residuals look like
  random scatter with no curvature, so the data show no sign of yielding
  over this strain range.
- **Repeatability:** The specimen-to-specimen spread is small: the
  coefficient of variation is at most 2.5% for any material.
  With only three specimens per material, the standard error of each mean
  is roughly SD/√3 ≈ 1 GPa.

## Per-specimen fits

| Specimen | Material | *E* (GPa) | Std. error of slope (GPa) | Intercept (MPa) | *R*² |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AL-1 | aluminum | 70.1 | 0.6 | -0.79 | 0.9995 |
| AL-2 | aluminum | 67.4 | 0.8 | 0.86 | 0.9988 |
| AL-3 | aluminum | 70.6 | 0.7 | -1.00 | 0.9991 |
| ST-1 | steel | 201.2 | 2.4 | -1.51 | 0.9988 |
| ST-2 | steel | 197.3 | 2.6 | 1.18 | 0.9986 |
| ST-3 | steel | 198.7 | 2.9 | 2.19 | 0.9984 |
| TI-1 | titanium | 114.6 | 1.9 | -0.02 | 0.9978 |
| TI-2 | titanium | 117.8 | 1.6 | -2.22 | 0.9985 |
| TI-3 | titanium | 117.2 | 1.5 | -0.08 | 0.9987 |

Full results: `results/moduli.csv` (by material) and
`results/moduli-by-specimen.csv` (by specimen).

    "aluminum": "68–72",

with open(SUMMARY_PATH) as f:
    summary = json.load(f)

materials = summary["materials"]
specimens = summary["specimens"]
strain_min, strain_max = summary["strain_range"]
n_points = specimens[0]["n_points"]
r2_min = min(s["r_squared"] for s in specimens)
max_abs_intercept = max(abs(s["intercept_mpa"]) for s in specimens)

    f"| **{m['modulus_mean_gpa']:.1f} ± {m['modulus_std_gpa']:.1f}** "
    f"| {m['modulus_min_gpa']:.1f}–{m['modulus_max_gpa']:.1f} "
    f"| {m['r_squared_pooled']:.4f} "

    f"| {s['modulus_se_gpa']:.1f} | {s['intercept_mpa']:.2f} "

{material_rows}

*Figure: Measured stress vs. strain for each specimen (markers) with the

## Discussion

- **Ranking:** {stiffest['material']} is the stiffest material, about
  {ratio:.1f}× stiffer than {softest['material']}. All three moduli fall
  within the typical handbook ranges for these materials.
- **Linearity:** Each specimen is well described by a straight line

| Specimen | Material | *E* (GPa) | Std. error of slope (GPa) | Intercept (MPa) | *R*² |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{specimen_rows}

Full results: `results/moduli.csv` (by material) and

"""

I set this up as a Calkit project with a two-stage pipeline. `calkit run` finished without errors, and I looked at the figure to check it.

## Results

| Material | E (GPa), mean ± SD of 3 specimens | Typical handbook value |
|---|---|---|
| Steel | **199.1 ± 2.0** | 190–210 |
| Titanium | **116.6 ± 1.7** | 105–120 |
| Aluminum | **69.4 ± 1.8** | 68–72 |

- **Fit quality:** each specimen fits a straight line very well (R² ≥ 0.998). The intercepts are within ±2.2 MPa of zero, so the lines pass close to the origin, as expected for elastic loading.
- **No yielding:** the data only go up to 0.2% strain, and from the plot I see no curvature or sign of yielding in that range.
- **Repeatability:** the spread between specimens is small, at most 2.5% for any material.
- **Pooled fit:** fitting all of a material's points together gives exactly the same slope as averaging the specimens, because every specimen was measured at the same strains.

## What's in the project

- **`analyze` stage** (`scripts/analyze.py`): fits a line to each specimen and to each material's pooled data. It writes:
  - `results/moduli.csv` (by material)
  - `results/moduli-by-specimen.csv`
  - `results/summary.json`
  - `figures/stress-strain.png`: all specimens, with each material's fit line labelled with its E. The figure is also registered in `calkit.yaml`.
- **`write-report` stage** (`scripts/write_report.py`): builds `report.md` from the results, so the numbers in the write-up always match the analysis. The report covers the method, a results table, the figure, a short discussion and a per-specimen table.
- **`main` environment:** a uv environment with pandas, numpy and matplotlib, defined in `requirements.txt`.

To rerun everything, use `calkit run`.

A few things to know:
- **Nothing is committed yet.** Calkit created the git repo, but I used `--no-commit`, so the files are only staged or untracked. Run `calkit save -am "Analyze elastic modulus"` (or just commit) when you're happy with them.
- **Handbook ranges are approximate.** They're general textbook values I put in for context, not taken from a specific standard. The titanium range assumes a typical alloy such as Ti-6Al-4V; commercially pure titanium is closer to 105 GPa.
- **Uncertainty is from only three specimens.** The ± values are sample standard deviations across three specimens per material.
